content: Lichen sclerosus, also referred to as lichen sclerosus et atrophicus (LSA) or white-spot disease, is a chronic, uncommon dermatological condition of unknown etiology. It is characterized by the appearance of white, atrophic patches on the skin, predominantly affecting the genital and perianal regions. These lesions may lead to scarring and significant discomfort. The condition was first described in 1887 by Dr. Hallopeau. In 1989, the International Society for the Study of Vulvovaginal Disease (ISSVD) officially adopted the term lichen sclerosus as the standardized medical nomenclature for this disease. Diagnosis of lichen sclerosus can be challenging and may require a skin biopsy to differentiate it from other conditions, such as condyloma. Histopathological findings typically include hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy, sclerosis of the dermis, and lymphocytic infiltration within the dermis. Epidemiologically, lichen sclerosus is more prevalent in women, particularly postmenopausal women, although it can also affect prepubertal girls. Men are less commonly affected, but when they are, the condition often manifests as whitish thickening of the foreskin, leading to phimosis. In men, this genital involvement is traditionally referred to as balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO). Non-genital skin involvement may present as porcelain-white plaques with follicular plugging and skin thinning. The disease can have a profound psychological impact on patients, often leading to feelings of depression, low self-esteem, and sexual dysfunction. Patients may benefit from support groups or counseling to address these emotional challenges. Support organizations, such as the National Lichen Sclerosus Support Group in the UK, provide valuable resources and a sense of community for affected individuals. The natural course of lichen sclerosus varies. While spontaneous remission is rare, particularly in young girls, the disease can persist for years. In vulvar cases, there is a 1-4% risk of progression to vulvar squamous cell carcinoma. In men, untreated lichen sclerosus is a significant cause of phimosis. Treatment typically involves the application of potent topical corticosteroids, which can alleviate symptoms and prevent further scarring. Other therapeutic options include cryotherapy and laser therapy. Regular follow-up is essential, as there is a small risk of malignant transformation within the affected areas.
